title: The cosine–sine decomposition
subtitle: G2 lecture 044000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Individually authored from the spoken lecture and its display-only mathematical appendix. Includes stepwise constructions, explicit hypotheses, worked examples and topic-specific vector figures; all slide prose is independent of audio.

slides.title: Understand two subspaces one principal plane at a time
slides.lead: In finite dimensions, principal vectors reduce the interaction of two projections to two-by-two blocks.
body: A tilted pair of lines spans a plane on which the projections have explicit cosine–sine matrices. Different principal pairs give orthogonal planes, so their contributions decouple.
Shared directions and right-angle defects sit in separate endpoint blocks. This decomposition turns geometric questions about subspaces into simple matrix calculations.
slides.takeaway: The cosine–sine decomposition separates the geometry into independent principal planes.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 044000 · Understand two subspaces one principal plane at a time

slides.title: One tilted pair
slides.lead: Take unit vectors e and f perpendicular to one another, and let v=c e+s f.
body: Here c=cosθ and s=sinθ with 0<θ<π/2. The projector P onto span(e) has matrix diag(1,0) in the basis (e,f).
The projector Q onto span(v) is vv*: multiplying the two-component vector (c,s) by its transpose gives the full two-by-two block.
slides.takeaway: Every nontrivial principal angle produces the same basic projection block.

slides.title: Check that Q really is a projection
slides.lead: The block formula is valid because c²+s²=1.
body: Multiplying Q by itself produces (c²+s²)Q=Q. Its transpose equals itself, so it is an orthogonal projector.
This local calculation is enough to verify the algebra of every nontrivial principal plane in the full decomposition.
slides.takeaway: Idempotence and self-adjointness come directly from scalar trigonometry.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 044000 · Check that Q really is a projection

slides.title: Build the perpendicular partner
slides.lead: Given a principal pair u in U and v in V, extract the part of v perpendicular to U.
body: Write c=⟨u,v⟩=cosθ>0 and s=sinθ>0. Set f=(v−cu)/s. Then f is a unit vector in U⊥ and v=cu+sf.
The normalization works because the squared perpendicular residual has length 1−c²=s². This construction explains where the second basis vector in each principal plane comes from.
slides.takeaway: A principal plane is generated by a principal vector and its normalized perpendicular residual.

slides.title: Why different principal planes are orthogonal
slides.lead: The SVD of the overlap map supplies paired principal vectors with vanishing cross terms.
body: Choose the u_i and v_i so that their inner products vanish across different indices. Then f_i=(v_i−c_i u_i)/s_i is orthogonal to u_j and f_j for j≠i.
Consequently each span(u_i,f_i) is orthogonal to the other principal planes, and both projections preserve every plane. Their matrices may be studied independently.
slides.takeaway: The SVD construction makes the principal-plane blocks mutually noninteracting.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 044000 · Why different principal planes are orthogonal

slides.title: Two angles in four dimensions
slides.lead: Take two orthogonal principal planes with angles thirty and sixty degrees.
body: Each plane carries its own P and Q block with its own cosine and sine. The full matrices are block diagonal, not coupled.
A vector whose components lie in both planes is projected by applying the thirty-degree formula on one block and the sixty-degree formula on the other. No cross-term appears.
slides.takeaway: Multiple principal angles correspond to independent two-dimensional blocks.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 044000 · Two angles in four dimensions

slides.title: The endpoint cases
slides.lead: The formula for f divides by sinθ, so θ=0 must be treated separately.
body: When θ=0, the direction is common to both subspaces and P=Q=1 on that line. When θ=π/2, source and target directions are orthogonal, and P and Q are complementary on the paired plane.
If dimensions differ, extra unpaired right-angle directions may remain. A complete decomposition includes these fixed endpoint blocks rather than forcing them into the nontrivial-angle formula.
slides.takeaway: Common directions and defects are genuine summands, not limiting generic blocks.

slides.title: Why doubled angles appear
slides.lead: The off-diagonal part of the tilted projection is c s.
body: Since 2cs=sin(2θ), block-off-diagonal quantities naturally contain a doubled angle. This is one geometric source of the sine-two-theta expressions in perturbation theory.
The identity does not by itself prove a perturbation theorem; it exposes the precise algebraic pattern that later spectral gap estimates control.
slides.takeaway: Double-angle functions arise from the mixed blocks of a projection.

slides.title: The balanced block theorem
slides.lead: When U and V both have dimension n inside a 2n-dimensional space, the blocks can be paired globally.
body: Under this balanced rank hypothesis, suitable orthonormal bases for U and U⊥ place the pair into a block form with diagonal C² and S² and mixed CS. The operators C and S are commuting nonnegative diagonal operators, with C²+S²=I.

If the subspace dimensions or endpoint multiplicities differ, extra blocks must be kept separately; the general Halmos decomposition records them rather than asserting a globally balanced representation.
slides.takeaway: The scalar principal-plane picture lifts to commuting operator blocks.

slides.title: Reconstruct one block
slides.lead: Start with v=cosθ e+sinθ f, then derive the rank-one projection onto v.
body: Check Q²=Q, compute its off-diagonal entry, and explain why that entry contains sin(2θ)/2. Then repeat the construction on two orthogonal principal planes.
Finally list what the formulas miss when θ is zero, θ is ninety degrees, or the subspaces have different dimensions.
slides.takeaway: The C–S decomposition is a geometric construction with an explicit two-by-two model.
